en: Śrīḥ.

The Karmanirṇaya, one of all the fundamental treatises composed by the venerable Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Salutations to the glorious Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is the very self of Śrī Hanumān, Abhinava Madhva, Antardhita Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.
Salutations to Him who is beloved by Ramā, the enjoyer of all sacrifices, and who is eternally worshipped by the gods, beginning with Vidhi, Īśāna, and Śakra.

He inserts the supplementary verses (upasargas) of the Mahānāmnīs. The first Mahānāmī is indeed this world; the second is the intermediate space; the third is yonder world. This Ṣoḍaśin-stotra is fashioned from all these worlds. In that he inserts the supplementary verses of the Mahānāmnīs, he fashions it from all these worlds. He who knows thus prospers by means of the Ṣoḍaśin, which has been fashioned from all the worlds.

He joins those prepositions which are subordinate elements of the *mahānāmnya* verses; he applies them. Those verses in which the name "Great" (*mahan*) is found are called *mahānāmnyaḥ*. The name of the Supreme Brahman, such as Indra and so forth, is "Great" (*mahat*) because of its great significance. For that Supreme Brahman is indeed great, due to the fulfillment of all attributes without exception. Regarding this, some say that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). That is not correct, because it contradicts both scripture and reasoning. Thus says the scripture: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"; "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss."
"He who is all-knowing is all-perceiving; his austerity consists of knowledge.
From him is born this Brahman, as well as name, form, and food.
For he is divine, formless, radiant, existing both within and without, and unborn."
"Indeed, he is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable.
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is even greater than that.
He who is our father and progenitor, the ordainer, who knows all abodes and all worlds."
"Full is that, full is this; from the full, the full arises.
When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains.
"He who possesses all names, all actions, all odors, and all tastes."
He has encompassed all this; he is beyond speech and beyond regard. "Now shall I proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms.
Increasing his body beyond all measure, they do not reach the limit of your greatness."
"There is no one, O Viṣṇu, who, being born or already born, has reached the furthest limit of your greatness," and so forth.
There is also logical reasoning: because He is the conscious creator of all, attributes such as omniscience and the like are logically established.
As stated in the Bhāgavata: "Because He is the agent, Brahman possesses qualities; [He is] the Person, the bull among men."
And it is not [the case that this is not supported],
for [it is said]: "The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading,
the inner self of all beings, the supervisor of actions, the dwelling place of all beings, the witness, the conscious, solitary, and devoid of qualities."

There is a contradiction with such [scriptural passages] as these, because of the statement therein that the qualities (guṇas) such as *sattva* and so forth are absent. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statements in [texts like] "The one God is hidden in all beings," which would imply that those [beings] also possess qualities. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*), for the very statement of its being "without distinction" is self-contradictory. If it is asked whether that [entity] is qualified by "being devoid of distinctions" or not: if it is unqualified, then there is no negation of distinctions; rather, it possesses distinctions itself. If it is qualified by that [absence of distinctions], then that [absence] itself is a distinction.

Furthermore, there is no proof for the state of being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*). Moreover, this contradicts the experience of scriptural statements regarding all distinctions and the arguments [supporting them]. Nor can it be [devoid of distinctions] while possessing false distinctions, because that would be a contradiction; for when one says "false distinction," it amounts precisely to saying "non-existent distinction. And thus, the very same fault stated against the position of [the Brahman] qualified by distinctions applies. Nor can it be [devoid of distinctions] while possessing indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) distinctions, because such an indeterminable thing is unestablished. Indeed, there is no perception of it there, and the word "false" (*mithyā*) denotes only non-existence, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for anything other than that.

Nor is there any other means of valid cognition [for such a thing], because it would contradict your own proposition. For nothing distinct from both the existent and the non-existent—namely, something characterized as neither existent nor non-existent—is established. When it is said, "it is not non-existent," two negations convey the original meaning with an intensification; thus, it becomes simply existent. Or, if one intends to express a specific distinction, it is "non-existent in another way."

Furthermore, what is this distinction? Is it difference (*bheda*), non-difference (*abheda*), or both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*)? It cannot be difference, because that is not admitted. Moreover, a merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) difference must be stated as being "inexpressible" (*anirvācya*) once [the reality] is established; yet there is nothing that is merely conventional. Nor is there any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the cessation of all conventional discourse. Furthermore, "conventionality" cannot be a common property (*sāmānya*) shared by both the false and the real, in the way that "smokiness" might be a common property of both smoke and vapor.

Nor can non-difference [of the two] be maintained, precisely because it is not admitted; likewise for both [the other alternatives]. Furthermore, if there were non-difference between the Brahman and the indeterminable [limiting adjunct], and between the two words denoting them, they would be synonyms. Nor is there ever a lack of synonymy based on a difference in what is excluded (*vyāvartya*), unless that difference in what is excluded introduces a distinction into the Brahman itself; if it does, then the sentence has a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭa-vākyārtha*). If it does not, then no second word need be uttered by one seeking knowledge of Brahman, as it would be irrelevant. Moreover, the existence of a false distinction has already been refuted. Consequently, there results either mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), infinite regress (*anavasthiti*), or a circular argument (*cakraka*). And the view that [Brahman] is distinct from both difference and non-difference is also rejected by the very same reasoning.

Regarding the phrase "distinct from the non-existent" (*riñcāsadvilakṣaṇam*), among [the meanings of] negation (*nañ*)—namely, absence, otherness, and opposition—what is the meaning here? If it is not absence, then the world would possess the nature of existence (*bhāvatva*) itself by virtue of being distinct from the non-existent. Nor is the world distinct from the non-existent as something other than the existent, because you do not admit attributes such as "being other than the non-existent" for either the non-existent or for Brahman; and furthermore, since the non-existent is admitted to be indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), there can be no distinction between that which is indefinable and the non-existent. Even so, if there were a distinction, the world would not be indefinable. Nor is it a case of opposition (*virodha*).

Because when one of two contradictory things is negated, the other is necessarily experienced; for when it is said that "what is non-existent does not exist," everyone in the world understands this simply as "it exists. Therefore, it is established that the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa possesses infinite attributes.

Nor does the non-establishment of God and so forth follow from the absence of the authority of a sentence regarding an already established fact, because there is no "thing to be done" (*kārya*) distinct from what is already established. Furthermore, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). For there is no such thing as "obligatoriness" (*kartavyatva*) other than being a means to a desired end, as there is no evidence for it. Moreover, it has been stated that the word [the Veda] does not express that [obligatoriness]. Since the optative suffix and the like have fulfilled their purpose by signifying being a means to a desired end, to postulate another "thing to be done" would involve the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanāgaurava*). Nor is there anything that necessitates such a postulation.

Furthermore, in the event of a disagreement, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated to establish that [meaning]; yet there is no inference (*anumāna*), because the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished. Nor is there presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there is no logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*). The claim that "the acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) occurs only with respect to what is connected to an action (*kārya*), precisely because of the absence of an action" is refuted from afar. For one who asserts that linguistic competency is toward what is connected to an action, what answer can be given when it is said that there is competency toward what is not connected to an action? If you say "it is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*"), the answer is "then let there be elision (*lopa*). Since all other words are already established, the elision of the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth alone is the more excellent solution.

Since children acquire linguistic proficiency through such expressions as "I laugh" (*hasāmi*) regarding an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*), and since there is no reason to abandon that [meaning] because it is the first to be encountered, and because proficiency is observed in exactly that way;
therefore, since validity is established for the accomplished fact, it is proven that Viṣṇu possesses great qualities.
Find it, O Maghavan; find the path, for you have praised the directions.
Bestow your aid, O Lord of powers, you who possess many riches among the ancient ones. 1.
And those [verses] begin with "O Maghavan, for you...
and so forth. O Maghavan—meaning either "O glorious one" or "O possessor of wealth"—"they call him 'Maghavan' by an indirect name, even though he is truly Makhavat (the possessor of sacrifice)."
"The gods, as it were, prefer what is out of sight and dislike what is manifest.

"Impel Indra with these [verses] to bestow wealth. "May that come to us for the sake of wealth. "Fame, indeed, is wealth. "You have attained wealth. "May wealth come to me. "You have attained wealth. "Wealth, indeed, is riches"—from such scriptural passages as these.

"May you know the way to praise"—having thus stated the general requirement for complete knowledge, he now prays for the specific purpose required at that moment: "Know the way. *Anuśaṃsiṣaḥ* means "you should point out"; *diśaḥ* means "paths," that is, instruct me yourself on the methods of praising you. *Pūrviṇām* refers to those who have come through the lineage of the Lord’s tradition for the sake of supreme knowledge. *Śacīnām*, meaning "of the powers," or "of the words," O Lord; O Master of Speech. *Puruvaso*, meaning "possessor of much wealth," or "possessor of much knowledge"; one who dwells in many things, or the abode of many. || 1 ||
O most wise one, awaken us with these our prayers;
O Indra, grant us food for the sake of glory, for you alone are the powerful one.

By these very invocations—by such searches for you and prayers to you—awaken, cause us to perceive, something of me and others, O Pracetasa! O Supreme Self, the Omniscient One of preeminent consciousness! For the sake of *dyumna* (splendor or knowledge), for wealth or fame, and for *iṣ* (food or nourishment), awaken us. For such indeed is Śakra; or rather, he is Śakra because he is the very embodiment of power (*śakti*). || 2 ||

O wielder of the thunderbolt, most powerful wielder of the thunderbolt, you are honored for wealth and for strength; O most bountiful wielder of the thunderbolt, you are honored—come hither, drink, and rejoice! 3.

For the sake of wealth, for gain, for strength, and for food—he who causes Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), to turn toward these is *vajrivāḥ*. Or, he goes as one who restrains [the senses]. *Śaviṣṭha* means most powerful or most blissful. *Ṛñjase*: you impel all [beings]. *Maṃhiṣṭha vajrin ṛñjase*—this repetition is for the sake of emphasis. *Matsva*: be exhilarated; bring about intoxication [of joy]. (3)
Grant us wealth and heroic strength; become the lord of spoils according to our desire.
O most generous wielder of the thunderbolt, you who are the mightiest among heroes, you are exalted. 4.

"Grant us wealth, bestow upon us heroic strength, and become the sustainer of our food and progeny"—for according to the Śruti, "Food is indeed progeny," and so forth. "According to their will" (*vaśāmanu*); from the verbal root *vaś* meaning "desire," *yathāvaśam* means "according to desire. He is the most powerful among the brave. (4)
He who is the most bountiful among the wealthy, O wise one, lead us toward him;
Indra knows that man, and I praise him, for he is the powerful lord. 5.

The greatest among the generous and glorious ones; the wise one, known as the "Doer" (kartar); lead us from all sides, everywhere. Indra has known it all; he has discerned it completely. Him alone do I praise. 5.
We invoke him for protection, the unvanquished giver;
may he carry us across our enemies—he who is wisdom, desire, and the great Truth. 6.

For protection, for preservation, or for the fulfillment of one's intentions; may He lead us across our enemies, adversaries, evils, or the darknesses. *Kratu* is of the nature of knowledge; *chandas* is of the nature of desire, so called because it is desirable (*chandya*) or because it covers (*chādana*). *Ṛtam* is that which is understood through the entirety of the scriptures. || 6 ||
We invoke Indra for the winning of wealth, the unconquered conqueror;
may he carry us across our enemies, may he carry us across our adversaries. 7.
For the sake of attainment and gain; from the destruction of existence. || 7 ||
O wielder of the stone, bestow upon us that bliss which you possess from of old;
O most powerful one, your bounty is praised, for the mighty Lord rules over all. 8.
Bestow upon us that excellent bliss which has existed from time immemorial through you; your fulfillment is praised. 8.
Surely you will place that new [hymn] within you, O Lord, slayer of Vṛtra, for the sake of the people.
Let us two speak together concerning those who are equal; he is a hero who goes among the cattle, a most gracious and guileless friend. 9.

That which is to be praised, that Brahman, you should properly establish within your heart. Through instruction for the sake of people, may you and I speak together regarding your own essential natures. He goes among the cows—that is, he becomes the object of knowledge—and is most gracious, supremely blissful, free from the need for further meditative concentration, and non-dual. || 9 ||

Come hither, indeed, come hither to Agni! Come hither, indeed, come hither to Indra! Come hither, indeed, come hither to Viṣṇu! Come hither, indeed, come hither, O Pūṣan! Come hither, indeed, come hither, O gods!
For such indeed is Śakra; for Śakra is the controller, he who acts according to his will. || 10 ||

The phrase "evāhyevaivāhi" emphasizes with great intensity the meaning already stated in the form of a dialogue among the deities beginning with Agni; for repetition signifies the intended meaning (*tātparya*). "Evāhi" means "evameva hi" (indeed, exactly so). As stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "But when the dialogue is firmly established, there is both division and the stage itself. Therefore, [it says] "agnāi" and so forth. "Evameva hi śakro vaśānanu" means that Śakra indeed acts according to his will, being independent (*svatantra*).
To Āya Manyāya, to Manyu, to Upomanyāya, and to Manyu.
May we approach with all-sustaining [offerings]. O Maghavan, know us! Vidoṃ! 11.

From the verbal root *aya* (meaning "to go"), *āya* is derived; *āyati* means "the future" or "that which is to be reached. The vowel *o* has the sense of "excess" (*atiśaya*), as in the word *upa*; there is a grammatical rule stating "o signifies excess. One who knows what is to be reached (*āya*) is *āyomanyaḥ*. One who knows even that which is nearby is *upomanyaḥ*. Because the other senses are turned away (*parāṅmukha*), they do not know the internal; this one, however, perceives even the internal through direct intuition (*aparokṣa*). Alternatively, *āya* refers to that which is to be reached by going (*ayana*) or movement, even if it is distant. From the verbal root *manu* (meaning "to understand"), *manyu* means "the knower."

The meaning of the intent is indeed this practice: "To the knower of the external, to the knower of the internal"—approach me with such a thought directed toward you who are centered in me. O Sustainer of the universe! Or rather: "To me, who perceives you both near and far, approach for the sake of my knowledge. Or: "Directed toward you, who know [all] from near and far, [I pray:
'Come, O Viṣṇu; I have no power to summon you; come to me.'"
"Thus Brahmā praised Viṣṇu, who was seated upon the lotus risen from his navel," so it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
"O All-pervading Lord, you who always meditate both nearby and afar,
come to me for the granting of knowledge"— thus did the son of Gāthī speak to Hari, according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
"In this world, Hari is always addressed as 'Om';
therefore, ascetics worship Him, the support of the universe," so it is stated in the *Mānasa-saṃhitā*.

The meaning of the passage, "Indra indeed fashioned the Great Self by means of these [ṛks]," is also explained in this very way. "Fashioning" (nirmāṇa) means the establishment of the Self through their exposition; for otherwise, they could not function as instruments.
"He who knows that alone shall be the father of his father"—so says the Śruti.

"Three steps have been placed in secret; he who knows that shall be the father of his father. "They are women, yet they call them males to me; he who has eyes may see them, but the blind man cannot discern them."
"Only that son who is a seer perceives these; he who understands them shall be the father of his father.
From such scriptural passages as these, it follows that consciousness alone is its creation:
"Indra produced one, Sūrya produced one, and from Vena they fashioned one by their own inherent power (*svadhā*)."

Or, it is the making known of such [meanings] as: *pracetana*, *pracetaya*; *āyāhi piba matsva kratuśchanda ṛtaṃ bṛhat sumna ādhehi no vaso*. These are prefixes (*upasarga*). Even parts [of words] become prefixes in relation to that which possesses those parts. They are called "prefixes" because they are prefixed (*upasṛṣṭatvāt*). A subordinate element (*upasarjana*) may be of two kinds: internal or external.
"In the *Śabdanirṇaya*, it is said: 'Just as in the case of *hastabaddha*, so too with words [joined] like prefixes. [Thus:
'He placed another [child] in his womb; love overflowed from him.'"
O wise one, bestow desirable wealth as a gift upon the one who praises you.
Impelled by us toward enlightenment, come, drink, and rejoice!
We embrace you—will-power, sacred meter, and the great cosmic order.

With the verse, "That gift of yours which bestows wealth—O Vasu, bestow favor upon us," he inserts [the word *upa*]. This praise of the Mahānāmnīs is performed for the purpose of showing that the insertion of the prefix *upa-* must be done even when the meaning of the entire Mahānāmnī is being recalled, provided it was not previously understood. Otherwise, apart from praising only that much, praising the entire Mahānāmnī would be redundant. According to the division of the three verses, there are three Mahānāmnīs: *vidā maghavan*, *samūtaye*, and *nūnam*. Regarding the first Mahānāmnī: "The terrestrial *hari* (Agni) is what is expressed by that first Mahānāmnī."
"In the second [verse] he is the lord of the atmosphere, in the third he is the lord of heaven," so it is said in the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā*.
"The three *mahānāmnī* verses consist of triplets; the first [of the *sāman*s] consists of five verses, the next of triplets, and the last of two verses;
the third [part] is joined with seven *nigadas*."
Thus there is a twofold division in rites such as recitation and meditation; and it is said in the *Pravṛtti*:
"The sacrifice of the *Ṣoḍaśī* was established by Hari, the lord of the three worlds.
Knowing Hari in this way and performing action for his sake, one is not born again."

The meaning of the prefix *eva* is also stated as being of the nature of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); therefore, it cannot be remembered without a thorough understanding of the previously mentioned meaning. Thus, one who knows this becomes possessed of half of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice when it is thus constructed.
"Forward [I send] for you the *triṣṭubh* hymn, the nourishment, for the exhilarating hero, for Indra.
With prayer and with wisdom, he seeks to win you for the attainment of the prize. (RV 8.97.1)

O Ṛtviks, bring forth! Indra, the Supreme Lord, desires to win over Soma through the *vastu*—the food known as the *triṣṭubh*, which bestows abundance. Through *purandhi*—his own intellect that takes refuge in the bodies of all living beings—and through the *triṣṭubh* being praised with ever-increasing excellence, it brings him great delight for the purpose of drinking the Soma. Thus, for that Hero, the Supreme Lord, the Soma is called *mandadvīra*, meaning "he who causes joy."

But he does not feel joy for his own sake; rather, it is "for your acquisition of the sacrifice" (*medhasātaye*), that is, for the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice. The plural "your" (*vaḥ*) is used out of respect toward the Lord, or it may refer to the Lord himself using the plural. In that case, the meaning is: "May this food, [which is] the *triṣṭubh* meter, be for the sake of the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice dedicated to you; may you cause it to flow forth abundantly. || 1 ||
Like the roar of flowing waters, like the roar of young women, you take heed of your lord, O inviolable cows. 2.

O waters, you who moisten—that is, those who cause wetting—you seek as your lord that Person, the filler, the one who causes overflowing; you become his consort. In every creation, you become the consort of whichever supreme being exists therein; this is why "the filler" (nadam) is mentioned again. You belong to the young women—the sky-dwelling ones who leap about, the inviolable ones in the form of smoke, the ageless ones in the form of seed, or the milch-cows who nourish the world (from the root *dhinv*, meaning "to nourish").

Or, according to the Vedic revelation beginning with "He dwells with thunder," you are the one who seeks [the favor of] Vāyu, the Lord of the cows—those "cows" being the inviolable (aghnyā) milch-cows that sprinkle with milk and move from place to place; for there is the Vedic text, "Vāyu indeed is the Lord of the cows," and because of the word *dhenu* itself. Or, you are the Lord of the "lowing" (*odatīnām*) ones—that is, those that sprinkle through speech—and of the "youthful" (*yoyuvatīnām*), meaning those that most excellently manifest their own nature, the "inviolable" (*anghyānām*) eternal milch-cows that nourish virtue, wealth, and pleasure; thus, you are the Lord of such Speech.

"One should worship speech as a cow; she has four udders: the utterance *svāhā*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance *hanta*, and the utterance *svadhā*. Two of her udders the gods subsist upon—the *svāhā* and the *vaṣaṭ*; humans [subsist upon] the *hanta*; and the ancestors [subsist upon] the *svadhā*. Her bull is the breath, and her calf is the mind. From such scriptural passages as these. (2)
These dappled cows, yielding milk for the preparation of the oblation, mix the Soma juice;
they are the clans at the birth of the gods, dwelling in the three luminous realms of heaven.

These speckled ones—whether they be waters, cows, or speech—mingle with the Soma of this *sūdadohas*, that is, of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which abides in Vāyu and is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). For the Soma becomes mixed with water, or it is "curdled" (*śrita*) by milk and the like, or it is grasped by means of mantras. This is also supported by the Śruti: "Now, the *sūdadohas*—the *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath. It is called *sūdadohas* because it milks out (*dogdhi*) excellent moisture (*sūda*), or ritual action and knowledge.

By means of this, a person rises up and becomes exalted; thus, *udaṃ* refers to knowledge and so forth, or to the mind. *Soma* is indeed speech, for they mix it with their own objects because of its fitness for inquiry; hence, speech is called *pṛśni*, either because it consists of praise or because it is worthy of praise. This worthiness of praise belongs equally to the waters and the cows at the birth of the gods—that is, at the sacrifice—for therein they are manifested, or [it refers to] prior knowledge. The *viśaḥ* (the common people) and the subjects also mix it; yet, since it is primarily they who mix it, the word "and" (*ca*) is omitted. [This occurs] in the three luminous realms of heaven.

Regarding the birth of the gods who abide as far as the sun, moon, and lightning—the sacrifice is indeed the birth of the gods, for therein the gods manifest themselves—according to such scriptural passages as: "From the sun and moon unto the lightning, these worlds are indeed supported. And:
"The sky is indeed the lightning; having approached its lord, Vāyu, she [the lightning] reaches the Supreme by that very means."
"Indeed, she shines in the world of Brahman," according to such scriptural passages; therefore, the lightning is indeed the celestial realm (dyu).
Worship him, worship him thoroughly; O Priyamedhas, worship him!
Let the sons also worship, and worship him boldly as one would a fortress. 4.

*Arcana* refers to sacrifice and the like; *prārcana* refers to knowledge, meditation, and the like, according to the Lord’s words: "The sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects, O scorcher of foes.

Perform the worship of those dear to sacrifice (*priyayajñāḥ*); perform the higher worship of those who possess dear knowledge (*priyajñānaḥ*); even you children (*putrakāḥ*) and the small-minded (*alpakāḥ*), perform worship!

And [it is said]: "The wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should not create a division of intellect among the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them to perform all actions.
By the word "uta" (also/even), it is indicated that even for the knowers of truth, worship is appropriate according to their respective stages of life (āśrama).
For the Śruti declares: "Therefore, O Viṣṇu, your praise is to be perfected even by the wise, and your sacrifice is to be accomplished by the one possessing oblations.
What is that which is to be worshipped? It is the bold (dhṛṣṇu), courageous (dhṛṣṭa) Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva. Do not worship the city, which is the body.

"O slender-waisted one, it is proper for the wise to mutually offer a respectful welcome, courtesy, and salutation toward another who is harsh of mind— toward that which dwells in the cave [of the heart] alone, and not toward the mere physical body," so it is said in the *Bhāgavata*.
"One should bow to Hari, whether with the body or alone;
never to the body, nor to that which is intent upon its pride," so it is stated in the Vyāsa-smṛti.
"Furthermore, one should worship" is the intended meaning. || 1 ||
The gargara resounds, the lizard croaks all around;
the piṅgā bird warbles nearby—for Indra, the sacred prayer is being raised. 5.

He states that even the sounds of the *gargara*, *godhā*, *piṅgā*, and so forth, being merely expressive of sound, denote the Blessed One himself, by means of the passage beginning with "ava svarāti gargaraḥ. The meaning is that all this is for Indra alone; the Veda (*brahma*) distinguishes [this] as being directed toward Indra alone. "Gargara" is the name for a foot-ornament, a large drum, a vessel of curd, and the trunk of an elephant. "Piṅgā" refers to the female *cakora* bird. The prefix *ava-* is used to indicate that even specific nuances such as diminution or excess are denotative of Him. "Can-iṣkadat" is an imitative sound (*anukāraśabda*), while "saniṣvaṇat" is used in the sense of intensity.

And the Śruti says: "All these Ṛg-verses, all the Vedas, and all sounds are indeed one single utterance (vyāhṛti), which is the vital breath (prāṇa) alone; one should know that the Ṛg-verse is the vital breath. Furthermore:
"The sound of churning curds is also, by its nature as an internal resonance (antarnāda), expressive of the terrifying power of Hari; for the internal resonance is indeed [the source of] terror."
One should likewise utter the "elephant-roar" (gajabṛṃhita) accompanied by the sound of "dhik";
because of its association with the *svarita* accent, the *svarita* occurs in the expression of "dhik".
One should utter such a great mantra joined with water and other substances.
"The ornament on the foot expresses reproach; that which is produced from it is said to be *svarita*.

The sound coming from a yellow-throated [peacock] indicates the state of being struck by wonder, and even another sound, that of the house-lizard, expresses that same state of wonder," so it is stated in the *Śabdatattva*. (2)
The far-reaching, well-yielding, and unswerving [cows] descend;
seize the Soma that flows forth for Indra to drink. 6.
And as for the roar of the river that comes rushing down, that defect denotes Indra;
for "the roars of rivers and oceans, because they are sounds, denote excellence;
indeed, sound (nāda) is expressive of excellence, and so too are other noises."
And for that purpose, rivers flow toward him:
"Having become the primordial source within the ocean, Hari, the destroyer of all, has acted with extreme speed;
he who is the submarine fire and the man-lion (Nṛhari) must be contemplated—he who gave water to the lowly and reduced [the world] to ashes."
Thus, in the Vaihāyasa-saṃhitā:

"The well-milking ones" means they are excellent performers of the milking of waters. "Without further throbbing" (anaparasphuraḥ) means there is no further pulsation or departure from them; they are of a nature that is eternally in motion. Because their throbbing has ceased, they seize the Soma; because of their immobility, [they seize] the mind (manas). || 3 ||
He who caused the well-yoked [horses] to gallop forth for the donor, he is the impeller, the leader, that very body, he who was released from the waters. 7.

He caused the *vyatīs*—the gods who are specifically superior—to spread out (*aphāṇayat*) for the sake of the donor, that is, the sacrificer, in his presence; [this is derived] from the root *phaṇ*, meaning "to expand. They were well-yoked and devoted to excellent yoga. Regarding them, it is said: "The *vyatīs* are remembered as deities who are specifically superior, eternally devoted to yoga, and solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa."
The Lord expands those very selves that constitute the sense organs;
indeed, it is the expansion of the power of the mind and other senses,
which is the manifestation of the deities brought about by Hari for the sake of His devotees.
Thus it is stated in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*;
and there is also the Vedic revelation: "With four [verses], he has spun out ninety names together, like a revolving wheel."

"May he, the knower of the mind, protect me with wisdom; O God, may I become a vessel for the immortal. May my body be capable of discernment; may my tongue be most sweet; and through my two ears, may I hear much. And in the *Mahābhārata*: "The gods do not protect one by taking up a staff like a cowherd;
rather, him whom they wish to protect, they endow with intelligence."

He is the *takvan*, the creator of the world—derived from the verbal root *tak* meaning "to create"—and because of such usages as, "The emission [of creation] cannot be turned back once impelled. He is also the leader of all; that very body of his is that which consists of the forms of both the creator and the leader of the world.

"In the Supreme Lord, there is no division between the body and the embodied, nor any division between the qualities and that which possesses them; for the Śruti declares, 'It is neither manifold here. Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa.
"By knowing That, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth."
"His body is bliss, His fragrance is happiness, His luster is knowledge, and He possesses true valor;

He is the knowledge of knowledge, the happiness of happiness—He is Viṣṇu, the supreme, the imperishable. This is also established by such scriptural passages. "By means of a garland of pure consciousness that shines with a multitude of variegated jewels..."
"In the *Puruṣottama-saṃhitā* it is said: 'The Lord, whose body is eternal bliss, is adorned by her who has revealed the true nature of the entire world.

[The word] *upamā* [is used] in the sense of comparison (*upamāyām*). In the context of comparison (*upamā-viṣaye*), he was 'released' (*amucyata*), meaning he became abandoned (*tyakta*), that is to say, peerless (*nirupama*)."

"Even when it is possible to express [the meaning] with few syllables, if one speaks with many syllables, there is here an excess of what has already been said; this constitutes a total prohibition [of such verbosity]," so it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. (1)
Truly, Śakra, Indra, has overcome all enemies;
he split apart the porridge being cooked within the mountain with his roar. 8.
Having transcended all enemies, ignorance, sin, and the like, Śakra-Viṣṇu indeed carries His devotees across.
"He whom this [Self] chooses, by him He is attained; to him this Self reveals His own form.
"I am the deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence for those [devotees]."
"I shall soon become [the refuge] for those who have fixed their minds on me, O Pārtha"—this and more is well known; he expresses this with the word *u*.
The meaning of the two words *ati* is that He has surpassed His enemies and has exalted Himself preeminently. The Blessed One shattered the bond, which is the object of the root *ud* in *odana*.
Bādarāyaṇa is the son of an unmarried woman; "the Supreme" refers to the Paramātman. At the time of its full ripening, that which is being cooked by speech alone—[as it is said:
"Indeed, at the time of ripening, through the union [of the teachings], the Blessed Vyāsa split open the *odana* (morsel) of karma being cooked by speech itself for his devotees without exception."
Thus, in the Vāyasa-saṃhitā, [chapter] 2.
Like a young boy mounting a new chariot, he,
of all-pervading power, mounted the winged buffalo-beast for his father and mother.

Standing like a child, he mounted a new chariot. The Youth (Kumāra) is the destroyer of the contemptible (the Māra). Like a child, his body is subtle; having abandoned each preceding body, he mounted each successive new body, taking the life-force (jīva) with him.

As it is said in the Mānya-saṃhitā: "Leaving behind the living body along with the life-force, the Imperishable Lord, having produced for the life-force a new body through its own power, enters [it]."

Or, "like a youth" means a child with a subtle body; or, "a child with a subtle body" does not mean a mere boy. He endowed him—who possessed wings [of virtue]—with qualities such as mature knowledge. Regarding the buffalo (mahiṣam), the great bowing one (mahānatam), Brahmā, the deer (mṛgam) who seeks his own self (mṛgayantam), he made him most skillful in action (vibhukratam) for his father, himself, his mother, and Lakṣmī. The meaning is that he again fulfilled the full knowledge (pūrmajñānam) concerning his father and mother. As it is said in the *Pravṛtta*: "Keśava, the great among the great, fulfilled his son Vidhātṛ—who was already full of knowledge—by granting him liberation. || 3 ||

They are known as they truly are. The attainment of the path consists in praising them as they are situated, without connecting them here and there. He who considers himself like one whose glory has departed should praise the *ṣoḍaśin* chant without interweaving it, lest he fall into distress on account of the meters. Now, he who desires to drive away evil should praise the *ṣoḍaśin* with interweaving; for man is indeed intertwined with evil. Thus, he drives away that very evil and impurity which is intertwined with him; he who knows this casts off evil.

"Pervaded" means entered into with distinction. "Unaltered" means unmixed. May I not fall into a state of misfortune—that is, a downward course—due to the suffering caused by reciting [the Veda] incorrectly or contrary to its established order. For it is said: "Recitation performed in reverse order brings victory over enemies; when mixed with other things, it destroys sin;
but when performed according to the established order, it bestows prosperity, even when one is engaged in reciting. Thus it proceeds.
"One who has lost his fortune should effect the loss of his own fortune and the destruction of another's sin;
one established in his station should effect the increase of fortune through the application of meters"—thus it is stated in the *Svādhyāyatattva*.
Furthermore: "In cases of 'something more,' 'both,' 'doubt,' and likewise 'similarity'..."

The word *iva* is employed by the learned even in the sense of "contempt," according to the *Śabdanirṇaya*. Therefore, the meaning is: "even when there is doubt regarding the attainment of fame. *Vihṛtam* means that which has been specifically gathered or joined together from here and there.
[It is said: "Because of the intermingling of evils, it is *vyatiṣakta* (interwoven) and destructive."
Through the entanglement of wealth, there is an entanglement that is indestructible;
for that which is similar [to another] becomes the destroyer of that very similar thing.
Thus, when wealth has reached its destruction, it is due to its own inherent power.
"One whose desire has increased cannot bring about the destruction of evil;
for desire does not lead to the destruction of wealth when it is conjoined [with other factors]"—thus it is said in the *Svādhyāyatattva*.

And since non-intermixture (*avyatiṣaktatva*) pertains to liberation (*mokṣa*), the word "as it were" (*iva*) here implies both meanings. By such a recitation, one destroys evil (*pāpmānam*); and also impurity (*śamalam*), such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, because evil is mentioned separately.
"Śamala is defined as sin, as well as passion, hatred, and the like;
they know offense to be śamala, and impurity (mala) also to be śamala"—thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.
He who meditates in this manner casts off evil from himself.
While the *ṛks* were being recited together, Janārdana was proclaimed as the specific destroyer of the sins accumulated by men;
and through His grace, even the state of being untainted by sin was attained by one who was liberated.

Nor is there a lack of validity for statements such as these with respect to their own meaning, because the validity of [statements] regarding established facts (*siddhārtha*) has been established, and because there is no contradiction. Nor is there any "complexity of assumption" (*kalpanā-gaurava*) in postulating an intention (*tātparya*) toward multiple meanings, since there is no assumption [of a new meaning] when the object is already apprehended through the words themselves. Furthermore, there is no distinction [to be made] that the literal meaning is not the intended meaning, for there is no evidence for such a claim.

In worldly sentences, where a sense intended by the author (*tātparyārtha*) is perceived as distinct from the literal meaning (*vācanikārtha*), the explicit wording itself is not the direct means of cognition; rather, that [intended sense] is known through inference based on the indicative mark of the words. Alternatively, when there is a contradiction, one resorts to a non-literal mode of operation (*amukhyavṛtti*), provided the speaker's reliability (*āptatva*) is certain. If the speaker's reliability is not certain, there is no validity at all. However, in the case of a Vedic sentence, no other sense is possible apart from the literal meaning. Nevertheless, among the many literal meanings, those that are not contradictory must be accepted.
The sūtra states: "It refers to either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or absorption (*sampatti*), for it is clearly revealed [in scripture].

"Because of dwelling (*vāsa*), because of procreation (*sūti*), because of shining (*devana*), because of dwelling (*vāsa*), because of splendor (*dyuti*), because of covering (*chādana*), or because of sporting (*krīḍā*);
because of strength (*bala*), because of not breathing (*asutva*), because of giving (*dātṛ*), and because of sustaining (*vartana*), the Vedas proclaim him as Vāsudeva."
And thus says the *Saukarāyaṇa-śruti*.

The word "either" (*anyatara*) is used precisely to dispel the doubt that liberation might be the same as deep sleep. "No meaning whatsoever pertaining to the Veda can exist without either conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or etymological derivation (*yoga*)."
"In that regard, the etymological (yaugika) sense is primary and exists everywhere, including in the Vedic;
however, the assumption of a conventional (rūḍha) meaning for an etymological term is for the sake of avoiding infinite regress.
Once [the etymology] is known, specific understanding and even linguistic usage proceed by way of convention," so it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*.

If one abandons the meaning explicitly stated in the text (*vācanika*) and instead postulates the meaning of a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*), then both the abandonment of what is heard (*śrutahāni*) and the postulation of what is not heard (*aśrutakalpanā*) result; thus, for him, these two faults—which are the most serious of all—are acquired in vain. And for one who speaks thus, what is the answer when it is said that injunctive words are either meaningless or that words denoting established facts (*siddha-śabda*) are authoritative regarding their own referents? There is no reason whatsoever for abandoning many meanings explicitly stated in the text. However, when a contradiction is perceived, another meaning must be accepted, even if it is merely explicit (*vācanika*). That too is established as being merely explicit for that very same reason.
Among all primary meanings, there exists a gradation;
therein, Hari alone is the supreme primary meaning denoted by all sounds.
The inclusion of other meanings occurs without contradicting those respective primary meanings.
"But when there is a primary contradiction with its own [literal] sense, another meaning must be abandoned in all cases;
this is the rule everywhere regarding the grounds of word, meaning, and knowledge.

Nor is it correct to say that a purpose exists only in the case of an action and not in the case of an established fact (*siddha*); for even in the case of mere knowledge, a great purpose is observed, as in the sentence concerning the father's being alive. And the Blessed One himself has said:
"There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the unchanging is called the imperishable.
But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self."
The imperishable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them;
because I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable.
Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as the Supreme Person—
he, O Bhārata, knowing all, worships Me with his whole being.
"Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by Me.
By understanding this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done, O Bhārata.
And: "The sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes, is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects."
"Indeed, meditation is superior to all actions, and from meditation comes supreme knowledge;
there is nothing equal to knowledge for the accomplishment of the goals of human life"—thus it is said. And also: "For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya."
"Even the entire multitude of all actions does not equal even a fraction of the fire of meditation upon Viṣṇu;
and that meditation on Hari is not fulfilled by even a ten-millionth part of the knowledge [of Him]," so it is said in the *Karmaviveka*.
"Only by knowing Him does one become immortal here; there is no other path for the journey."
And such is the Śruti.

Nor does the Veda terminate in mere ritual action, because the purpose is precisely the knowledge of bliss. Therefore, only that which is already established [as an end] possesses the status of being a purpose. Furthermore, the intended meaning of eulogies and the like has been explained by the Lord himself as not departing from the literal sense of the words.
"Or [the statement] is figurative because of the lack of self-knowledge; for thus the scripture shows.

Therefore, those things such as praise which appear to be contradictory should be construed with reference to the requirements of the auxiliaries to knowledge. However, when there is a contradiction with the Śruti and other authorities, even a secondary (gauṇa) meaning is appropriate for the Purāṇas and similar texts.
"Deceit, sorcery, and contradictory practices..."
"O Maheśvara, having shown yourself to all people, quickly delude them," and so forth, in the Vārāha [Purāṇa]. ||| 6 ||
Rising to the realm of the sun, let us go to Indra’s dwelling;
having drunk of the honeyed draught, let us dwell together thrice seven times at the station of our friend. 1.

"Having drunk the soma-juice, Indra and I shall ascend to the celestial realm (*viṣṭapa*) of the sun, the *brandha* heaven; there, in that abode of Indra known as *brandha-viṣṭapa*, we two shall dwell together and experience happiness. Thus it proceeded: "In the twenty-one divine stations of his friend Indra—the wielder of the discus (*cakrin*) and the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*)—those places are enjoyed even by his devotees, according to the ritualists."
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, you have drunk the pressed juices of the ancestors; now this libation is yours alone.
Drink the honeyed Soma, O Indra; O bull, pour it all at once into your belly. 2.

O *harivaḥ*—you who turn the *hari*s (the bay steeds), that is, the senses, toward the Soma juices belonging to the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) which you have previously drunk; or alternatively, you who proceed with the *hari*s. This midday libation (*mādhyandina-savana*) is yours alone. Furthermore, the word *atho* indicates a different sense: shower (*āvṛṣasva*), that is, pour down, the honeyed Soma into your belly, and rejoice along with our protection (*satrā*). The word *pīta* (drunk) is used here like the word *pīta* (yellow/golden); because there was no prior drinking, that very act of drinking is primary, hence the use of the word *pīta*.

Because it belongs exclusively to Indra, the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) is exclusive; "it has exhilarated" refers to the third pressing, for there indeed exhilaration occurs preeminently due to fulfillment. Thus is the sixteenfold cup (*ṣoḍaśin*) characterized by the three pressings. It contains the word *vṛṣan* because it is especially dear to the bull-like Indra. Thus is the sixteenfold cup characterized by four forms. He prospers; he becomes successful.

But when the wings have been spread out, one should chant by half-verses, interposing the feet [of the subsequent verses]. The joints of the preceding [verses] are their feet. Gāyatrīs are joined with Paṅktis; of the Paṅktis, however, two feet remain, and with those two one should utter the *praṇava*. Uṣṇihs are joined with Bṛhatīs; of the Uṣṇihs, one should make the last two feet [of each] into two [separate feet], making the first [foot] four syllables long.

Having divided the two-footed verses into four parts, one should place the first [part] with *triṣṭubh* verses, the subsequent [parts] with *jagatī* verses, and the fourth syllable of the last [verse] as the first syllable of the preceding one, thereby forming an *anuṣṭubh*; thus one should recite those that are not in their original meters. One should place [the parts] from the end of the third feet of the second and third [verses]. With the words "pracotana" in the preceding [verse], and "pracetaya" in the succeeding [verse]; in the subsequent [verses], having made the other feet the sixth [feet], one should chant them in the manner of an *anuṣṭubh*.

He inserts five-syllable prefixes into the eleven-syllable feet of the Mahānāmnī verses; for this Ṣoḍaśin-stotra is constructed from all the meters. In that he inserts five-syllable prefixes into the eleven-syllable feet of the Mahānāmnī verses, he thereby constructs it from all the meters. He who knows thus prospers by means of the Ṣoḍaśin-stotra, which has been constructed from all the meters.

He prefixes five syllables that are not *upasarga*s to the *mahānāmnī* verses in their eleven-syllable quarters: "Evā hy evā apāḥ pūrvoṣām harivaḥ sutānām; evā hīndra atho idam savanam kevalam te; evā hi śakro mamaddhi somam madhumantam indra; vaśī hi śakraḥ satrā vṛṣan jaṭhare āvṛṣasva."
Furthermore, action should be performed preceded by devotion, knowledge, and dispassion toward the Blessed Lord:
"The deluded, considering sacrificial rites and public works to be the highest, do not know any other good;
having experienced the fruit of their merit on the back of heaven, they enter this world or one even lower."
"Even actionlessness does not shine if it is devoid of devotion to the Infallible; how much less so the stainless knowledge that is merely free from taint?
How much more so action that is not offered to the Lord—even if it be performed without motive—and which is eternally unwholesome?
For from Him comes the activity of all beings, and by Him all this is pervaded."
"By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.

"Those learned in the three Vedas, drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped Me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven. Having reached the holy world of the Lord of the Gods, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven."
"Having surrendered all actions to Me with a mind focused on the Self,
being free from desire and the sense of 'mine,' fight, freed from fever.
Those men who constantly follow this teaching of Mine..."
"Those who possess faith and are free from malice are liberated even from their past actions.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded in all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of discernment."

"Ascetics devoted to charity, illustrious, high-minded, knowers of the mantras, and most auspicious—even they find no security without surrendering to Him; salutations again and again to that Subhadraśravas.
"He who knows this is indeed a giver."

"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful. "Not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings, they are of vain hopes, vain actions, vain knowledge, and devoid of discernment."
"Listen again to my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets.
Since you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit:
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me."
"You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me.

This is established by such scriptural and traditional (smṛti) passages as: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss; it is the gift and the supreme goal of the giver who abides in that knowledge."... and so forth.
Homage to Nārāyaṇa, whose feet are ever-worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, Uṣṇīṣa, and the Sun; to the glorious one, who is most beloved.
Thus ends the *Karmanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Thus concludes the Determination of Action.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
May this Samaputa have been well-composed by me,
the one named Prabhañjana, through the grace of the feet of Ramā and the Lord of Ramā.
